issues.legal_issue: A child adopted by the widow of a deceased coparcener may become a coparcener and claim a share in continuing joint family property held by the sole surviving coparcener, because the property’s passage by survivorship does not constitute vesting or divesting for the purpose of the statutory restriction on divesting a vested estate.
material_facts: Two brothers were coparceners, and when one died without children, the joint family properties remained with the surviving brother, who became the sole surviving coparcener.
The deceased brother’s widow remained alive and had a right to maintenance from the joint family properties.
After the adoption law came into force, the widow adopted a child as the son of herself and her deceased husband.
The adopted child and the widow brought a suit seeking partition and separate possession of a share in the properties.
issues.conclusion: The adopted child became a coparcener in the joint family and was entitled to seek partition and a share in the properties that remained joint family property. The statutory restriction against divesting an estate already vested in another person did not bar the claim, because survivorship did not vest the joint family property in the sole surviving coparcener in the relevant sense.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 12 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, an adopted child becomes the child of the adoptive family from adoption, subject to the proviso that the child must not divest an estate vested in another person before adoption. Sections 11, 12 and 14 support the conclusion that a child adopted by a widow becomes a member of the family of her deceased husband. Joint family property does not cease to be joint family property when held by a sole surviving coparcener; its passage by survivorship does not involve the vesting or divesting contemplated by section 12(c). The Court followed Gowli Buddanna v. Commissioner of Income Tax, Mysore, Bangalore, Sitabai v. Ram Chandra, and Vasant v. Dattu; it approved Y.K. Nalavade v. Anand G. Chavan, distinguished the relevant observations in Sawan Ram v. Kala Wanti as obiter, and overruled Narra Hanumantha Rao v. Narra Hanumayya.

predicates.partition_suit: A widow and a child adopted by her bring a proceeding seeking partition of family property.
predicates.widow_has_maintenance_right_from_joint_p: The deceased coparcener’s widow remains alive and has a right to maintenance from the family property.
predicates.property_remains_joint_family_property_w: Family property remains joint family property while held by the sole surviving coparcener.
predicates.widow_adopts_child_as_member_of_deceased: The widow adopts a child as a member of the family of her deceased coparcener husband.

issues.definition: When a partition suit is brought in these circumstances, the adopted child is entitled to a share in the property that remains joint family property.

issues.legal_issue: An alienation of joint family property made by a sole surviving coparcener before another coparcener is born or adopted remains effective against that later coparcener.
material_facts: Before the widow adopted the child, the sole surviving coparcener had sold two items of the joint family property to third parties for consideration.
The partition decree excluded those items from the property available for partition.
issues.conclusion: The adopted coparcener could not claim a share in the items alienated before the adoption; the prior alienations stood.
issues.legal_principle: A sole surviving coparcener may dispose of coparcenary property as if it were separate property while he remains the sole surviving coparcener. A coparcener born or adopted afterward cannot object to an alienation made before that birth or adoption. The Court applied the principle stated in Vasant v. Dattu.

predicates.partition_suit: A later coparcener seeks a share in family property in a proceeding for partition.
predicates.sole_survivor_alienates_joint_property_b: The sole surviving coparcener transfers family property before another coparcener is born or adopted into the family.

issues.definition: If the sole surviving coparcener alienates family property before a later coparcener joins the family, the alienation remains effective against that later coparcener.
